findings.trigger: release_gift() acquires LOCK at line 194 and, whenever the version has not already been decided as 'passed' (i.e. on the very first startup for a version, and on every later startup for a version already decided 'granted', per the function's own documented behaviour), calls service.power_gift(...) at line 202. That call (not shown in this section, but named 'power_gift' on ProgressService, the class this module was split out of) is what delegates to grant_power_gift(), which itself does 'with LOCK:' again at line 88. If LOCK (imported from services.mech.progress_service, not part of this section) is a plain threading.Lock rather than a re-entrant threading.RLock, this second acquisition by the same thread deadlocks - which would hang release_gift(), and with it whatever startup or scheduled path calls it, on essentially every DDC start.
findings.suggestion: Confirm in services/mech/progress_service.py that LOCK is a threading.RLock (or otherwise re-entrant). If it is a plain Lock, restructure release_gift so it does not hold LOCK across the nested call into power_gift/grant_power_gift, or make grant_power_gift's own locking conditional on the caller not already holding it.
findings.unsure_why: The definition of LOCK lives in services/mech/progress_service.py, which is not part of this review section, so I could not confirm whether it is re-entrant. Given how central and frequently-exercised this startup path is, a plain Lock here would very likely already have been caught by the project's own tests, so a re-entrant lock is the more likely explanation - but I cannot verify that from the material given.

findings.trigger: get_comprehensive_data() reads mech state three separate times instead of once: core_data comes from mech_service.get_mech_state_service() (line 274), _calculate_evolution_data() independently calls progress_service.get_state() again (line 568) to derive level_name/next_level/thresholds, and _calculate_power_bars() independently calls progress_service.get_state() a third time (line 887) for the Power/Evolution bar numbers. If a donation (and possibly a level-up) is booked by another thread between these reads, the single MechDataResult returned to the caller can mix pre- and post-donation values - e.g. current_level from the older read next to a level_name, next_level or power bar computed from the newer one - and this mismatched result is cached for up to 10 seconds (the cache TTL) and handed to every caller during that window.
findings.suggestion: Fetch the mech/progress state once at the top of get_comprehensive_data() and pass that single snapshot into _calculate_evolution_data() and _calculate_power_bars() instead of letting each helper read the state again on its own.
findings.unsure_why: services/mech/mech_service.py and services/mech/progress_service.py are not part of this section, so I could not confirm whether their reads are backed by one lock/snapshot in a way that rules out observing different states microseconds apart, or how often donations actually land concurrently with a comprehensive-data read in practice.

findings.trigger: get_evolution_info() computes 'progress_to_next' as (total_donations - current_threshold) / (next_threshold - current_threshold) * 100 with no try/except around the function body (unlike its sibling functions in this file). If the operator's own config/mech/evolution.json ever gives two consecutive levels the same 'cost' value - easy to do by accident when hand-editing costs in the web panel or the file - a mech sitting at the lower of those two levels hits (next_threshold - current_threshold) == 0 and the call raises an uncaught ZeroDivisionError.
findings.suggestion: Guard the division (e.g. treat next_threshold == current_threshold as 'no more progress to show', similar to the level-11 case) or wrap the computation in the same style of try/except used elsewhere in this module.
findings.unsure_why: I could not see this function's callers in this section - get_evolution_level_info()/mech_data_store.py use a different ('unified') path for the data shown in the panel, so get_evolution_info() may or may not still be on a live code path. If it is dead code, this never fires.

findings.trigger: calculate_dynamic_cost(level, member_count) looks up the level via get_evolution_level_info(level); if that lookup returns falsy (the level is simply missing from base_evolution_costs - for example an operator's own <config dir>/mech/evolution.json was written before a later DDC release added a new level, or an entry was deleted by mistake while editing), the function returns (0, 1.0) at line 391 - the exact same result it returns for the legitimately-free level 1 - with no error, warning, or log line distinguishing 'not configured' from 'free by design'. A mech could reach that level for $0.00 with nothing in the logs pointing at why.
findings.suggestion: Distinguish the 'no such level configured' case from 'level 1 is free': log an error and refuse the level (or fall back to a real, clearly-marked cost) instead of silently returning 0.

findings.trigger: get_canvas_size_for_resolution(level, 'big') scales both dimensions by the big/small size ratio at line 235 (`return (int(270 * ratio), int(base_height * ratio))`), but the two comment lines directly above it (233-234) say the opposite: 'we use native resolution after smart cropping - Don't scale the canvas, let it be the natural size'. Whichever of the two is the actually-intended behaviour, the other is currently wrong: callers requesting the 'big' canvas size get a canvas scaled by `ratio`, even though the adjacent comment says they should get the untouched native size.
findings.suggestion: Resolve the contradiction: either remove the scaling (to match the comment) or correct/remove the comment so it matches what the code does, so the next person touching this doesn't rely on the wrong one.
findings.unsure_why: The comment and the code directly contradict each other, which is certain; what I can't tell from this section is which of the two is the intended behaviour, since the actual renderer/caller that consumes this canvas size is outside this section.

notes: Two smaller observations that did not meet the bar for a formal finding: (1) services/mech/mech_high_res_service.py's small_adjustments dict in _get_cropping_adjustments (private helper, not a PLAN.txt name) only covers levels 1-10, while the sibling small_walk_heights dict in get_canvas_size_for_resolution covers 1-11; level 11 (OMEGA MECH) silently falls back to {top:0, bottom:0}. This may well be intentional (level 11's own sprite dimensions might not need pre-cropping) rather than an oversight, so I did not raise it as a finding. (2) EvolutionConfigService._get_fallback_config()'s community_size_tiers only defines a single 'MEDIUM' tier; if evolution.json fails to load at the moment a cost is calculated (I/O error, corrupted JSON), every community size - not just medium ones - would transiently be costed as 'MEDIUM' with no error surfaced. This only applies during a load failure of the operator's own file, and I did not have enough context on how often that path is actually hit to call it a finding rather than a defensive fallback doing what fallbacks do.
